title: Poor Proxies #5: The Finish Line Fallacy
author: Jamie Clark
summary: Part five of Jamie Clark's 'Poor Proxies for Learning' series tackles what he calls the Finish Line Fallacy — the widespread assumption that because content has been delivered, it has been learned. Drawing on Rob Coe's framework of poor proxies (developed alongside the 2014 Sutton Trust report What Makes Great Teaching?), Clark argues that curriculum coverage is a record of what was taught, not what was retained, and that treating the end of teaching as the end of learning structurally produces forgetting. He grounds the argument in two foundational cognitive science findings: Robert Bjork's work showing that conditions which make learning feel fluent in the moment (clear explanations, organised notes) produce the most fragile memories, and Graham Nuthall's landmark research showing students typically need three to four encounters with a concept — in different contexts — before it reliably transfers to long-term memory. A coverage-driven curriculum, by definition, provides one encounter per topic and then moves on. The practical consequences are severe: gaps go undetected, vulnerable students are carried forward without the foundations they need, and curriculum planning optimizes for delivery rather than retention. Clark offers five strategies to move beyond the fallacy: spaced retrieval built into every lesson, checks for learning rather than completion, deliberate planning for multiple encounters with key ideas, daily review as a standing structure, and reframing the end of a unit as a diagnostic moment rather than a signal to move on. The article's core reorientation is the distinction between two questions: 'Have I covered this?' and 'How do I know students have learned this?' — and the insistence that only the second one produces reliable evidence.
points: Bjork's distinction between storage strength and retrieval strength is the cognitive-science underpinning of the whole argument: a lesson can be followed perfectly — with high retrieval strength in the moment — and produce almost no durable storage strength, meaning students remember nothing a week later despite having 'understood' in class.

Nuthall's finding that students need three to four encounters in different contexts before content reliably transfers to long-term memory is a structural indictment of coverage-driven curriculum design, which by definition provides one encounter and then moves on to new material.

The Finish Line Fallacy has disproportionate costs for the students who most need support: when coverage is assumed to equal learning, gaps go undetected, and students who were confused or lacked prerequisite knowledge at the first encounter are carried forward without the foundations the next unit requires.

Spaced retrieval built into every lesson — two or three questions from last week, one from last month, one from last term — is the highest-leverage structural response to the fallacy; five minutes per lesson compounds into substantial durable retention across a year.

The decisive reorientation is from delivery to retention as the unit of success: 'Have I covered this?' is the wrong question because it tracks teacher behaviour; 'How do I know students have learned this?' is the right question because it demands evidence of change in student long-term memory.
quotes: The Finish Line Fallacy is what happens when we treat the end of teaching as the end of learning. It is the assumption that because content has been delivered — explained, discussed, demonstrated, and worked through — students have learned it. The curriculum has been covered. The finish line has been crossed.
Delivery is not the same as learning. Presentation is not the same as understanding. And the fact that content has been taught tells you almost nothing about whether it has been retained.

Storage strength, the depth at which something is embedded in long-term memory, is not the same as retrieval strength, how readily it comes to mind right now. A student can follow a lesson perfectly and remember almost nothing a week later. Coverage, in other words, is a record of what was taught — not of what was learned.

Most of what students are taught is forgotten within days or weeks. Students need to encounter content multiple times, in different ways, before it becomes a permanent part of their knowledge. — Graham Nuthall, The Hidden Lives of Learners (2007)

When coverage is the measure, teachers design for delivery and often teach to the test. The focus becomes getting through the content — ensuring every topic is addressed, every concept explained, every skill demonstrated. But when coverage becomes the goal rather than the prerequisite, something important gets lost: the time and design required for students to actually learn and revisit what has been taught.

The Finish Line Fallacy also matters because of what it does to the students who most need support. When coverage is assumed to equal learning, gaps go undetected. Students who did not understand the first time — who were confused by the explanation, who lacked the prior knowledge to make sense of it, who were distracted at the critical moment — are carried forward into the next unit without the solid foundations of knowledge they need.

This is why the question at the end of every unit should never be 'Have I covered this?' — it should always be 'How do I know students have learned this?' Those are two very different questions. And only one of them produces reliable evidence.
